'''''Gone Home''''' is a [[First-person (video games)|first-person]] [[walking simulator]] [[video game]] developed and published by [[Fullbright (company)|The Fullbright Company]]. ''Gone Home'' was first released for [[Microsoft Windows]], [[OS X]], and [[Linux]] computers in August 2013, followed by console releases for the [[PlayStation 4]] and [[Xbox One]] in January 2016, the [[Nintendo Switch]] in September 2018, and [[iOS]] in December 2018.

Set in the year 1995, ''Gone Home'' puts the player in the role of a young woman returning from overseas to her rural Oregon family home to find her family currently absent and the house empty, leaving her to piece together recent events. ''Gone Home'' does not feature much interactivity, but instead has the player explore the house at their own pace and determine what has transpired by examining items, journals, and other items left around the various rooms. The Fullbright team, having previously worked on ''[[BioShock 2: Minerva's Den]]'', took concepts and ideas from that game to craft an exploration game to engage the player in uncovering the narration by non-linear progression by searching the house, while keeping the project manageable for their small team.

''Gone Home'' received generally positive reviews at release.

== Gameplay ==
The player takes the role of Katie in the [[First-person (video games)|first-person]] view, who can move around the house and view and interact with objects. There are no defined goals in the game; however, the game encourages and rewards the player when they explore new areas of the house and search for new messages. Much of the interactivity rests upon looking at objects and notes within the house. In order to progress in the game, the player must find certain objects that unlock access to other parts of the house.

== Plot ==
[[File:Gone Home - Launch Trailer.webm|thumb|left|thumbtime=69|The launch trailer sets the scene for the game.]]

On 7 June 1995, 21-year-old Katie Greenbriar (voiced by [[Sarah Elmaleh]]) returns home from overseas to her family's new home in fictional Boon County, Oregon. Her family consists of her father, Terry, a failed writer who makes a living reviewing home electronics; her mother, Janice, a [[wildlife conservation]]ist who recently got promoted to director; and her 17-year-old sister Samantha (voiced by Sarah Grayson). Upon arriving, she finds the house deserted, much of their possessions still in moving boxes, and a note on the door from Sam imploring Katie not to investigate what happened.<ref name=ign-2012/><ref>{{cite news|title=Gone Home transports players back to 1995|url=http://www.eurogamer.net/articles/2012-11-15-gone-home-preview-an-authentic-look-back-at-1995|first=Jeffrey|last=Matulef|date=15 November 2012|work=[[Eurogamer]]|access-date=15 January 2013|archive-date=26 March 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140326234508/http://www.eurogamer.net/articles/2012-11-15-gone-home-preview-an-authentic-look-back-at-1995|url-status=live}}</ref>

Searching the house, Katie begins to piece together what happened during her absence. After moving in, Samantha found it difficult to adjust to her new high school, but eventually made friends with another girl, Yolanda "Lonnie" DeSoto, a [[Junior Reserve Officers' Training Corps|JROTC]] cadet. The two bonded over ''[[Street Fighter]]'', [[punk rock]], [[grunge]] and the burgeoning [[riot grrrl]] movement, and after sneaking off to a concert, the two became romantically involved. After various incidents at school, Sam's parents found out about her relationship, forbade Sam to close her bedroom door while Lonnie was over, and went into denial that their daughter is a lesbian. As Lonnie was set to eventually ship out to begin her service, Sam was left distraught.

Two days after her farewell show, which coincides with the day of Katie's homecoming, and the week of Sam's parents going on a vacation (which is revealed to actually be a [[Couples therapy|counseling]] trip instead of a camping trip, as they told others), Lonnie departed to her station, but eventually called Sam from a payphone to tell her that she got off the bus in [[Salem, Oregon|Salem]] and she wanted them to be together. Sam's final journal entry to Katie explains that she packed up her things and took her car to find Lonnie, hoping to start a new life with her outside of Oregon. But she promises that she will one day see her again.

Optionally, Katie can find various other clues that provide information on additional events that happened during the time: it is implied that Janice was beginning to have romantic feelings towards a subordinate, and that Terry was berated by his father via letter about his failed writing work, as well as Sam and Lonnie's suspicion that the house was haunted by the deceased Oscar Masan, Terry's uncle and former owner of the house. It is also implied that Terry's decision to write about a character traveling back in time to 1963 to stop the [[Assassination of John F. Kennedy|Kennedy assassination]] may have been influenced by his own sexual abuse by Masan, which either occurred or ended in 1963, when he was 13 years old.

== Development ==
[[File:The_Fullbright_Company_-_Game_Developers_Choice_Awards_2014.jpg|thumb|right|The Fullbright Company at the [[Game Developers Choice Awards]] in 2014. From left, Kate Craig, Steve Gaynor, Johnnemann Nordhagen and Karla Zimonja]]
[[Fullbright (company)|Fullbright]] was founded by Steve Gaynor, Karla Zimonja, and Johnnemann Nordhagen as "The Fullbright Company". The three had previously worked together at [[2K Games]] on ''[[BioShock 2: Minerva's Den]]''. All three were drawn by the prospect of developing an exploration game influenced by ''Minerva's Den'' through a small [[independent video game development|independent team]] rather than a large company, and subsequently left 2K Games to form Fullbright.<ref name="polygon fullbright"/><ref name="pcgamer 2013"/> To reduce costs, the team moved into a house together in [[Portland, Oregon]], and set up the office in the basement, with ''Gone Home'' being their first game.<ref name="polygon fullbright"/><ref name=EdgeProfile/> Gaynor considered their previous work on the ''BioShock'' games as effectively the pre-production stage for ''Gone Home'', allowing them to complete it within seventeen months.<ref name="pcgamersn 2017"/> The rapid development was aided by first prototyping the game in ''[[Amnesia: The Dark Descent]]''{{'}}s [[HPL Engine 2]] (which Gaynor had prior experience with), before completing the game in the [[Unity (game engine)|Unity 4]] [[game engine]].<ref name=JoystiqEngine>{{cite web| url=http://www.joystiq.com/2013/10/24/gone-home-began-as-an-amnesia-mod-and-you-can-play-it/| title=Gone Home began as an Amnesia mod, and you can play it| author=Danny Cowen| work=[[Joystiq]]| date=24 October 2013| access-date=3 November 2013| archive-date=8 July 2014| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140708214252/http://www.joystiq.com/2013/10/24/gone-home-began-as-an-amnesia-mod-and-you-can-play-it/| url-status=live}}</ref> The game's budget was less than $200,000.<ref>{{cite web|first=Todd|last=Martens|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/90549126/the-los-angeles-times/|title=Game Changers|newspaper=[[Los Angeles Times]]|page=49|date=March 4, 2014|accessdate=December 14, 2021|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|archive-date=14 December 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211214150247/https://www.newspapers.com/clip/90549126/the-los-angeles-times/|url-status=live}}</ref>
 
The initial concept for ''Gone Home'' was for the player to explore a [[Home automation|smart house]] that included a central [[artificial intelligence]] running everything with robots running around to complete tasks. The player would have been able to change the state of the house through their actions; Gaynor compared this idea to a non-combative ''[[System Shock]]'' game. As they explored this idea, and recognizing the small size of their team, they considered what would change if they made the house more like a regular household without any other characters visibly present, which significantly simplified the development into something more manageable for the team. This created the focus of the game as being "no other people, no other characters, [just] you in a single environment".<ref name=EdgeProfile>{{cite magazine| title=Studio Profile: The Fullbright Company| author=Edge staff| magazine=[[Edge (magazine)|Edge]]| issue=259| date=November 2013| pages=114–117}}</ref> The reduced scope allowed them to complete the game with the three of them for programming, narrative, and 2D art assets, along with remote work from Kate Craig for the game's 3D modeling. Particularly, the smaller scope eliminated the need for any type of character modeler or animator.<ref name="pcgames 2015">{{Cite web | url = https://www.pcgamesn.com/gone-home/the-making-of-gone-home | title = The making of: Gone Home | first = Joe | last = Donnelley | date = 2 October 2015 | access-date = 15 August 2018 | work = [[PCGamesN]] | archive-date = 22 August 2017 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20170822134920/https://www.pcgamesn.com//gone-home/the-making-of-gone-home | url-status = live }}</ref> Craig's wife [[Emily Carroll]], a comic artist whom Gaynor was a fan of, also assisted by designing some of the game's art asset and logos.<ref name="polygon fullbright">{{cite web | url = https://www.polygon.com/features/2013/8/13/4568900/the-fullbright-company-gone-home | title = Meet Me In Portland: The Fullbright Company's Journey Home | first = Mike | last = Mahardy | date = 13 August 2013 | access-date = 16 August 2018 | work = [[Polygon (website)|Polygon]] | archive-date = 17 August 2018 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20180817023027/https://www.polygon.com/features/2013/8/13/4568900/the-fullbright-company-gone-home | url-status = live }}</ref>

Narratively, ''Gone Home'' was designed around family; Gaynor had stated that for all the science fiction trappings of ''Minerva's Den'', its core narrative was about a man, his wife, and how the man's past was affecting that relationship, and used the same approach for ''Gone Home''. They placed the player as one of the members of the family to remove any type of morality of exploring a house that did not belong to them. Additionally, they established that the family had only recently moved into the home; Gaynor had worried that the player would have difficulty identifying key elements that would be present among all the other objects within a well lived-in home, while within a recent move, only objects of immediate importance would have been unpacked, making it easy for the player to focus on these.<ref>{{cite web | url = http://gamasutra.com/view/news/198340/How_Gone_Homes_design_constraints_lead_to_a_powerful_story.php | title = How Gone Home's design constraints lead to a powerful story | first = Leigh | last = Alexander | date = 15 August 2013 | access-date = 15 August 2018 | work = [[Gamasutra]] | archive-date = 15 August 2018 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20180815232818/http://gamasutra.com/view/news/198340/How_Gone_Homes_design_constraints_lead_to_a_powerful_story.php | url-status = dead }}</ref> Fullbright set the game in 1995 because they considered it the most recent year in which technology had not made the majority of communication digital in nature, so that they did not have to account for how digital communication would affect their storytelling, while still keeping elements of the game familiar to players.<ref name=ign-2012>{{cite news|title=Gone Home is Undiluted Adventure|url=http://ca.ign.com/articles/2012/11/15/gone-home-is-undiluted-adventure|first=Charles|last=Onyett|date=15 November 2012|work=[[IGN]]|access-date=15 January 2013|archive-date=23 October 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131023141651/http://www.ign.com/articles/2012/11/15/gone-home-is-undiluted-adventure|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="pcgames 2015"/> Another source of inspiration was [[urban exploration]], particularly Japanese ''haikyo'', homes long abandoned due to industrialization. Gaynor said there were mysteries about its residents that people could put together from examining the state of the abandoned home.<ref>{{cite web | url = https://kotaku.com/how-modern-japanese-ruins-inspired-a-computer-game-5935262 | title = How Modern Japanese Ruins Inspired a Computer Game | first = Brian | last = Ashcroft | date = 16 August 2012 | access-date = 16 August 2018 | work = [[Kotaku]] | archive-date = 16 August 2018 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20180816194545/https://kotaku.com/5935262/how-modern-japanese-ruins-inspired-a-computer-game/ | url-status = live }}</ref>

Gaynor stated that ''Minerva's Den'' was more focused on environmental storytelling than action-driven gameplay, and set the approach and necessary design elements they needed for ''Gone Home''.<ref name="pcgamersn 2017">{{cite web | url = https://www.pcgamesn.com/bioshock-infinite/gone-home-tacoma | title = The BioShock games were pre-production for Gone Home | first = Jeremy | last = Peel | date = 9 August 2017 | access-date = 9 August 2017 | work = [[PCGamesN]] | archive-date = 9 August 2017 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20170809211917/https://www.pcgamesn.com/bioshock-infinite/gone-home-tacoma | url-status = live }}</ref> Other elements that informed ''Gone Home'' from their ''BioShock'' experience was non-linear levels to explore, and discovering narrative elements through audio logs that the player would have to actively seek out, both which supported the exploration elements of the game.<ref name="pcgamer 2013">{{cite web | url = https://www.pcgamer.com/gone-home-steve-gaynor-interview/ | title = Gone Home interview with Steve Gaynor: BioShock, the '90s, and what makes a "game" | first = Tyler | last = Wilde | date = 5 April 2013 | access-date = 15 August 2018 | work = [[PC Gamer]] | archive-date = 10 November 2019 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20191110192959/https://www.pcgamer.com/gone-home-steve-gaynor-interview/ | url-status = live }}</ref> Gaynor also considered the approach that [[Looking Glass Studios]] used for developing [[immersive sim]]s.<ref>{{Cite web | url = https://www.polygon.com/features/2015/4/6/8315901/looking-glass-gone-home | title = The Looking Glass Philosophy Behind Gone Home | first = Mike | last = Mahardy | date = 6 April 2018 | access-date = 17 August 2018 | work = [[Polygon (website)|Polygon]] | archive-date = 17 August 2018 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20180817231116/https://www.polygon.com/features/2015/4/6/8315901/looking-glass-gone-home | url-status = live }}</ref> One challenge that Fullbright considered was that not every player would necessarily find every narrative clue for the various plot elements, and so it was necessary for them to make the story flexible enough that the player could understand these narratives without necessarily seeing every element they designed.<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.nytimes.com/2013/08/19/arts/video-games/in-gone-home-a-family-mystery-unfolds.html | title = Student's Trip Ends; A Mystery Just Begins | first = Chris | last = Sullentop | date = 18 August 2013 | access-date = 16 August 2018 | work = [[The New York Times]] | archive-date = 17 August 2018 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20180817023122/https://www.nytimes.com/2013/08/19/arts/video-games/in-gone-home-a-family-mystery-unfolds.html | url-status = live }}</ref> Gaynor was aware this approach to a game would be considered unconventional, so they did not set out to make something avant-garde but instead more as a proof of concept that such games could be immersive to draw the player in to fully explore and come to understand the narrative themselves.<ref name=ign-2012/>

[[File:Gone Home - Zine.png|thumb|right|The player explores objects around the house to piece together the story. Much of the game's art is influenced by the [[riot grrrl]] movement of the mid-1990s.]]
The game features music from the [[riot grrrl]] bands [[Heavens to Betsy]] and [[Bratmobile]]; Fullbright knew of their Portland-based label [[Kill Rock Stars]], and worked early on with them to secure the rights to the music once they had settled on the locale and time period.<ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.pcgamer.com/2013/03/21/gone-home-trailer-announces-music-from-90s-riot-grrrl-bands/ | author=Wilde, Tyler | title=Gone Home trailer announces music from '90s riot grrrl bands Heavens to Betsy and Bratmobile | work=[[PC Gamer]] | date=21 March 2013 | access-date=5 April 2013 | archive-date=11 April 2013 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130411014826/http://www.pcgamer.com/2013/03/21/gone-home-trailer-announces-music-from-90s-riot-grrrl-bands/ | url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.motherjones.com/media/2013/09/gone-home-women-in-video-games/ | title = Why This Indie Game Studio Chose a Feminist Drama Over Guns and Zombies | first = Matt | last = Connelly | date = 20 September 2013 | access-date = 16 August 2018 | work = [[Mother Jones (magazine)|Mother Jones]] | archive-date = 16 August 2018 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20180816230616/https://www.motherjones.com/media/2013/09/gone-home-women-in-video-games/ | url-status = live }}</ref> After showing the game at Grrrl Front Fest, a Portland riot grrrl music festival, it attracted the attention of a local band, The Youngins, who went on to provide the music for Girlscout, the fictional band in the game.<ref name=EdgeProfile/><ref name=music>{{cite web | url=http://thefullbrightcompany.com/2013/08/14/the-music-of-gone-home/ | author=Gaynor, Steve | title=The Music of Gone Home | publisher=The Fullbright Company | date=14 August 2013 | access-date=16 August 2013 | archive-date=18 August 2013 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130818195248/http://thefullbrightcompany.com/2013/08/14/the-music-of-gone-home/ | url-status=live }}</ref> The game's original musical score was composed by [[Chris Remo]], Gaynor's friend and co-host from the ''[[Idle Thumbs]]'' podcast, and featuring over 30 minutes of music that accompany the game's main exploration gameplay, with unique music also scored to each of the game's audio logs.<ref name=music/>

A [[developer commentary]] mode was added as a free update to the game in October 2013.<ref name=IGNCommentary>{{cite web| url=http://uk.ign.com/articles/2013/10/22/gone-home-updated-with-new-commentary-mode| title=Gone Home Updated With New Commentary Mode| author=Marty Sliva| work=[[IGN]]| date=24 October 2013| access-date=3 November 2013}}</ref>

=== Ports ===
A console version of the game was in development by Midnight City; however, this was later cancelled following Midnight City's closure in March 2015.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Matulef|first1=Jeffery|title=Gone Home is no longer in development for consoles|url=https://www.eurogamer.net/articles/2015-03-03-gone-home-is-no-longer-in-development-for-consoles|website=Eurogamer|date=3 March 2015|access-date=4 March 2015|archive-date=5 March 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150305172901/http://www.eurogamer.net/articles/2015-03-03-gone-home-is-no-longer-in-development-for-consoles|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.gamespot.com/articles/gone-home-console-version-canceled/1100-6425677/|title=Gone Home Console Version Canceled|access-date=16 March 2021|archive-date=8 November 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201108103023/https://www.gamespot.com/articles/gone-home-console-version-canceled/1100-6425677/|url-status=live}}</ref> Later, the development of the console port for [[PlayStation 4]] and [[Xbox One]] were switched to [[Majesco]], and were released on 12 January 2016. These ports included enhanced graphics and audio, and used the updated [[Unity (game engine)|Unity 5]] game engine.<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.destructoid.com/gone-home-going-to-xbox-one-and-ps4-in-january-324818.phtml | title = Gone Home going to Xbox One and PS4 in January | last = Holmes | first = Jonathan | date = 7 December 2015 | website = [[Destructoid]] | publisher = [[ModernMethod]] | access-date = 7 December 2015 | archive-date = 10 December 2015 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20151210032755/http://www.destructoid.com/gone-home-going-to-xbox-one-and-ps4-in-january-324818.phtml | url-status = live }}</ref>

''Gone Home'' received "generally favorable" reviews, according to [[review aggregator]] [[Metacritic]].<ref name="MCPC" />

Emily Morganti for ''[[Adventure Gamers]]'' commented that ''Gone Home'' had a "realistic, engrossing story that's beautifully told through environmental clues and audio narration" and that "many people read books for the opportunity to see life through someone else's eyes, but it's rare for a game to do it as well as this one does."<ref name="AdventureGamers"/> The ''[[Financial Post]]''{{'}}s Matthew Braga also noted that "This is a game that some will hold up as forward-thinking evidence in the ongoing debate of games-as-art", adding that the game was made to "plumb the depths of experience outside of gaming's typically targeted white, male, youthful core."<ref name="FinancialPost"/> However, ''[[Eurogamer]]'' editor Oli Welsh stated "The Fullbright Company has built a fine house for intimate storytelling in games, but it hasn't found the story to live in it yet."<ref name="Eurogamer"/>

The game's LGBT themes were praised.<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.polygon.com/2013/8/19/4627606/opinion-finding-someone-like-me-in-gone-home | title = Opinion: Finding someone like me in Gone Home | first = Danielle | last = Riendeau | date = 19 August 2013 | access-date = 15 August 2018 | work = [[Polygon (website)|Polygon]] | archive-date = 16 August 2018 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20180816025550/https://www.polygon.com/2013/8/19/4627606/opinion-finding-someone-like-me-in-gone-home | url-status = live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url = http://www.slate.com/blogs/outward/2013/11/12/video_games_embrace_gay_romance_from_the_ballad_of_gay_tony_to_the_last.html | title = The Gaying of Video Games | first = Terry | last = Mulcahy | date = 12 November 2013 | access-date = 15 August 2018 | work = [[Slate (magazine)|Slate]] | archive-date = 15 August 2018 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20180815232928/http://www.slate.com/blogs/outward/2013/11/12/video_games_embrace_gay_romance_from_the_ballad_of_gay_tony_to_the_last.html | url-status = live }}</ref> Fullbright reported receiving numerous feedback not only from LGBT players of the game that appreciated how they told the story and how such people have to do deal with rejection by their family, but also from players who had opposed LGBT rights who found the game presented the issues related to LGBT to change their mind on the subject.<ref name="pcgames 2015"/> Fullbright also received some criticism from players for focusing on LGBT themes at the expense of other story elements.<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2014/apr/10/sharing-joysticks-how-video-games-are-opening-up-to-lgbt-themes | title = Sharing joysticks: how video games are opening up to LGBT themes | first = Tim | last = Bowers | date = 10 April 2014 | access-date = 15 August 2018 | work = [[The Guardian]] | archive-date = 15 August 2018 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20180815200956/https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2014/apr/10/sharing-joysticks-how-video-games-are-opening-up-to-lgbt-themes | url-status = live }}</ref> Due to statements made by the organizers of [[PAX (event)|PAX Prime]] that Fullbright considered derogatory towards LGBT, the company pulled out of showing ''Gone Home'' at the Indie MEGABOOTH showcase during the 2013 PAX Prime event, stressing the importance of respecting LGBT issues.<ref name="TFC20130621">{{cite web|last=Gaynor|first=Steve|title=Why we are not showing Gone Home at PAX|url=http://thefullbrightcompany.com/2013/06/21/why-we-are-not-showing-gone-home-at-pax/|date=21 June 2013|access-date=16 August 2013|archive-date=12 August 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130812060656/http://thefullbrightcompany.com/2013/06/21/why-we-are-not-showing-gone-home-at-pax/|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="Gamasutra20130621">{{cite web|last=Ligman|first=Kris|title=Gone Home devs pull out of PAX Indie Megabooth|url=http://www.gamasutra.com/view/news/194849/Gone_Home_devs_pull_out_of_PAX_Indie_Megabooth.php|publisher=Gamasutra|date=21 June 2013|access-date=16 August 2013|archive-date=11 May 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140511110135/http://www.gamasutra.com/view/news/194849/Gone_Home_devs_pull_out_of_PAX_Indie_Megabooth.php|url-status=dead}}</ref> In the wake of this, PAX announced that it would establish Diversity Hubs at its future events for "attendees to find information related to issues surrounding women, LGBTQ, people of color, disabled people, and mental health issues in gaming".<ref>{{Cite web | url = https://www.gamespot.com/articles/pax-addresses-inclusivity-with-addition-of-diversity-lounges/1100-6416795/ | title = PAX addresses inclusivity with addition of "Diversity Lounges" | first = Eddie | last = Makuch | date = 4 April 2014 | access-date = 15 August 2018 | work = [[GameSpot]] | archive-date = 15 August 2018 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20180815201134/https://www.gamespot.com/articles/pax-addresses-inclusivity-with-addition-of-diversity-lounges/1100-6416795/ | url-status = live }}</ref>

Some reporters have considered the question of whether ''Gone Home'' should be considered a video game, as it lacks the normal interactivity one would normally have with a video game.<ref>{{cite magazine | url = https://www.wired.com/2013/08/gone-home-review/ | title= Gone Home: A Videogame, Without All That Pesky Videogame In The Way | first=  Chris | last= Kohler | date= 15 August 2013 | access-date = 15 August 2018 | magazine = [[Wired (magazine)|Wired]]}}</ref> Gaynor asserted that ''Gone Home'' was specifically developed for the video game medium, stating that they considered it an "edited discussion" between Fullbright and the player, as "[t]he content that you encounter appears differently than for someone else. It is unique to each user and their interpretation. The interactivity of it makes the experience unique to yourself."<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.polygon.com/2014/3/31/5566098/gone-home-is-it-a-game | title = When is a game not a game? | first = Brian | last = Crecente | date = 31 March 2014 | access-date = 15 August 2018 | work = [[Polygon (website)|Polygon]] | archive-date = 16 August 2018 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20180816025445/https://www.polygon.com/2014/3/31/5566098/gone-home-is-it-a-game | url-status = live }}</ref><ref name="pcgamer 2013"/> Gaynor used the example of the ability to turn lights on or off in any room in the house as an example of this. They included this interactivity as they had developed the game, they found that this gave a means for players to track if they had been within a room before or not, since the house starts otherwise dark, so he considered this one method by which they know what players would likely want to do and providing them means for them to do that, thus making the experience interactive.<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.gamedeveloper.com/design/what-makes-i-gone-home-i-a-game- | title = What makes Gone Home a game? | first = Brandon | last = Sheffield | date = 20 March 2014 | access-date = 15 August 2018 | work = [[Gamasutra]] | archive-date = 16 August 2018 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20180816000844/https://www.gamasutra.com/view/news/213612/What_makes_Gone_Home_a_game.php | url-status = live }}</ref> The lack of interactivity led to ''Gone Home'' to be called "walking simulator" at its release, though since then, the industry has come to accept "walking simulators" to describe similarly contemplative narrative games with little direct interactivity, like ''[[The Stanley Parable]]'', ''[[Firewatch]]'', and ''[[What Remains of Edith Finch]]''.<ref>{{cite news | url = https://www.rockpapershotgun.com/2014/06/28/walking-simulator-proteus-ed-key-ricky-haggett/ | title = Self-Interviewing Devs: Proteus And "Walking Simulators" | first = Alice | last = O'Conner | date = 28 June 2014 | access-date = 15 August 2018 | website = [[Rock Paper Shotgun]] | archive-date = 15 August 2018 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20180815201041/https://www.rockpapershotgun.com/2014/06/28/walking-simulator-proteus-ed-key-ricky-haggett/ | url-status = live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.salon.com/2017/11/11/a-brief-history-of-the-walking-simulator-gamings-most-detested-genre/ | title = A brief history of the "walking simulator," gaming's most detested genre | first = Nicole | last = Clark | date = 11 November 2017 | access-date = 15 August 2018 | work = [[Salon (magazine)|Salon]] | archive-date = 24 August 2020 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20200824042010/https://www.salon.com/2017/11/11/a-brief-history-of-the-walking-simulator-gamings-most-detested-genre/ | url-status = live }}</ref> ''Gone Home''{{'}}s approach to exploratory storytelling was a point of influence for parts of ''[[Uncharted 4: A Thief's End]]'' and ''[[Prey (2017 video game)|Prey]]''.<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.polygon.com/2016/4/4/11358228/uncharted-4-preview-single-player-story-hands-on-madagascar-ps4 | title = Uncharted 4 shines by making time for the quiet moments | first = Samit | last = Sarkar | date = 4 April 2016 | access-date = 16 August 2018 | work = [[Polygon (website)|Polygon]] | archive-date = 16 August 2018 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20180816230522/https://www.polygon.com/2016/4/4/11358228/uncharted-4-preview-single-player-story-hands-on-madagascar-ps4 | url-status = live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.vice.com/en/article/how-the-queer-indie-game-gone-home-influenced-prey/ | title = How the Queer Indie Game 'Gone Home' Influenced 'Prey' | first = Danielle | last = Riendeau | date = 24 May 2017 | access-date = 16 August 2018 | work = [[Vice (magazine)|Vice]] | archive-date = 16 August 2018 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20180816232026/https://waypoint.vice.com/en_us/article/8x4j5b/how-the-queer-indie-game-gone-home-influenced-prey | url-status = live }}</ref> ''[[Polygon (website)|Polygon]]'' named ''Gone Home'' among the most important games of the 2010s for its unique approach of conveying plot through examining objects, and its focus on [[queer]] relationships.<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.polygon.com/2019/11/13/20963006/gone-home-most-important-game-of-the-decade | title = Why Gone Home is the most important game of the decade | first = Nicole | last = Carpenter | date = November 13, 2019 | access-date = November 13, 2019 | work = [[Polygon (website)|Polygon]] | archive-date = 22 April 2023 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20230422101633/https://www.polygon.com/2019/11/13/20963006/gone-home-most-important-game-of-the-decade | url-status = live }}</ref>

Due to both the atypical nature of ''Gone Home'' and its narrative centered around LGBT issues, it became a central point of discussion at the onset of the [[Gamergate controversy]] in August 2014. A portion of video game players, some who supported the Gamergate movement, criticized games like ''Gone Home'' and ''[[Depression Quest]]'' for lacking the qualities of normal video games while earning praise from the gaming press, as well as including topics like LGBT issues. Critics countered that these elements are part of considering [[video games as an art form]], demonstrating how the medium is changing.<ref>{{cite news | url = https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/act-four/wp/2014/10/29/gamergate-reopens-the-debate-over-video-games-as-art | title = Gamergate reopens the debate over video games as art | first = Alyssa | last = Rosenberg | date = 29 October 2014 | access-date = 15 August 2018 | newspaper = [[The Washington Post]] | archive-date = 20 July 2018 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20180720022449/https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/act-four/wp/2014/10/29/gamergate-reopens-the-debate-over-video-games-as-art/ | url-status = live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.nytimes.com/2014/10/26/opinion/sunday/the-disheartening-gamergate-campaign.html | title = Can Video Games Survive? | first = Chris | last = Sullentop | date = 26 October 2014 | access-date = 15 August 2018 | work = [[The New York Times]] | archive-date = 26 October 2014 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20141026062144/http://www.nytimes.com/2014/10/26/opinion/sunday/the-disheartening-gamergate-campaign.html | url-status = live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web | url = https://www.polygon.com/2018/9/7/17827216/gone-home-nintendo-switch-steve-gaynor-interview | title = As Gone Home turns five, we look back at its polarizing legacy | first = Allegra | last = Frank | date = 7 September 2018 | access-date = 7 September 2018 | work = [[Polygon (website)|Polygon]] | archive-date = 7 September 2018 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20180907224843/https://www.polygon.com/2018/9/7/17827216/gone-home-nintendo-switch-steve-gaynor-interview | url-status = live }}</ref>

===Sales===
By September 2013, Fullbright announced that the game had sold more than 50,000 copies.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://thefullbrightcompany.com/2013/09/11/updates-ign-fantastic-fest-indiecade-and-initial-sales-numbers/|title=Updates: IGN, Fantastic Fest, Indiecade, and initial sales numbers|last=Gaynor|first=Steve|date=11 September 2013|work=The Fullbright Company|access-date=12 September 2013|archive-date=16 September 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130916213125/http://thefullbrightcompany.com/2013/09/11/updates-ign-fantastic-fest-indiecade-and-initial-sales-numbers/|url-status=live}}</ref> By February 2014, sales had reached 250,000 copies.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.joystiq.com/2014/02/06/gone-home-finds-250k-sales-most-on-steam/?ncid=rss_truncated|title=Gone Home finds 250K sales, most on Steam|last=Conditt|first=Jessica|date=6 February 2014|work=[[Joystiq]]|publisher=[[AOL]]|access-date=7 February 2014|archive-date=26 June 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140626134124/http://www.joystiq.com/2014/02/06/gone-home-finds-250k-sales-most-on-steam/?ncid=rss_truncated|url-status=live}}</ref> By the time of release of ''[[Tacoma (video game)|Tacoma]]'', Fullbright's second game released in October 2017, ''Gone Home'' had sold more than 700,000 copies.<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.pcgamer.com/gone-home-prevented-tacoma-from-being-judged-on-its-own-says-creator-steve-gaynor/ | title = Gone Home prevented Tacoma from being judged on its own, says creator Steve Gaynor | first = Joe | last = Donnelley | date = 3 October 2017 | access-date = 15 August 2018 | work = [[PC Gamer]] | archive-date = 6 July 2018 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20180706104234/https://www.pcgamer.com/gone-home-prevented-tacoma-from-being-judged-on-its-own-says-creator-steve-gaynor/ | url-status = live }}</ref>

===Awards and accolades===
The game was also nominated for "Excellence in Narrative" for the [[Independent Games Festival]] for 2013.<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.gamasutra.com/view/news/188908/Road_to_the_IGF_The_Fullbright_Companys_Gone_Home.php | title = Road to the IGF: The Fullbright Company's Gone Home | first = Leigh | last = Alexander | date = 20 March 2014 | access-date = 16 August 2018 | work = [[Gamasutra]] | archive-date = 16 August 2018 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20180816230549/https://www.gamasutra.com/view/news/188908/Road_to_the_IGF_The_Fullbright_Companys_Gone_Home.php | url-status = dead }}</ref>

''[[Polygon (website)|Polygon]]'' named ''Gone Home'' their Game of the Year for 2013.<ref name="Polygon 2014-01-15">{{cite web |url=http://www.polygon.com/2014/1/15/5311568/game-of-the-year-2013-gone-home |title=Polygon's 2013 Game of the Year: Gone Home |first=Christopher |last=Grant |work=[[Polygon (website)|Polygon]] |date=15 January 2014 |access-date=15 January 2014 |archive-date=27 May 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140527120118/http://www.polygon.com/2014/1/15/5311568/game-of-the-year-2013-gone-home |url-status=live }}</ref>

''Gone Home'' was nominated for several categories at the 2014 [[Game Developers Choice Awards]], including "Game of the Year", "Innovation Award", "Best Narrative", and "Best Downloadable Game", while Fullbright won as a studio for "Best Debut" for ''Gone Home''.<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.engadget.com/2014/01/09/gone-home-the-last-of-us-tearaway-top-gdc-award-nominations/ | title = Gone Home, The Last of Us, Tearaway top GDC Award nominations | first = Dave | last = Hinkle | date = 9 January 2014 | access-date = 16 August 2018 | work = [[Engadget]] | archive-date = 17 August 2018 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20180817024702/https://www.engadget.com/2014/01/09/gone-home-the-last-of-us-tearaway-top-gdc-award-nominations/ | url-status = live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.engadget.com/2014/03/20/papers-please-and-the-last-of-us-honored-at-gdc-awards-show/ | title = Papers, Please and The Last of Us honored at GDC awards show | first = Ludwig | last = Kietzman | date = 20 March 2018 | access-date = 16 August 2018 | work = [[Engadget]] | archive-date = 17 August 2018 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20180817023123/https://www.engadget.com/2014/03/20/papers-please-and-the-last-of-us-honored-at-gdc-awards-show/ | url-status = live }}</ref>

During the [[17th Annual D.I.C.E. Awards]], the [[Academy of Interactive Arts & Sciences]] nominated ''Gone Home'' for "[[D.I.C.E. Award for Outstanding Achievement for an Independent Game|Downloadable Game of the Year]]".<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.interactive.org/games/video_game_details.asp?idAward=2014&idGame=1325 |title=D.I.C.E. Awards By Video Game Details Gone Home |publisher=[[Academy of Interactive Arts & Sciences]] |website=interactive.org |access-date=27 November 2023}}</ref>

The game won the 2013 [[British Academy Games Awards]] for best "Debut Game" while nominated for "Best Story".<ref name="BBC 2014-03-12">{{Cite web | url = https://www.bbc.com/news/technology-26549269 | title = Bafta games: The Last of Us clears up at awards | first = Dave | last = Lee | date = 12 March 2014 | access-date = 12 March 2014 | publisher = [[BBC]] | archive-date = 13 March 2014 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20140313013453/http://www.bbc.com/news/technology-26549269 | url-status = live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url = http://static.bafta.org/files/games-nominations-2014-2166.pdf | title = BAFTA Video Game Awards - Nominations | date = 12 February 2014 | access-date = 12 February 2014 | publisher = [[BAFTA]] | url-status = dead | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20140222214648/http://static.bafta.org/files/games-nominations-2014-2166.pdf | archive-date = 22 February 2014 }}</ref>
